questions.title:
What exactly is the reference policy $
abla$ used in DPO and when is $
abla$ equal to the SFT model?
questions.question_body: The paper frequently refers to a reference policy $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ (often the SFT model $\pi^{\text{SFT}}$). I'm confused about the exact role of $\pi_{\text{ref}}$. Is it always the SFT model trained on preferred completions? If the SFT model isn't available the paper says we set $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ by maximizing likelihood on preferred completions. How is that different from simply doing Preferred-FT? Why is that chosen as the reference rather than e.g. an un-finetuned LM or the empirical distribution of all generated samples?

questions.title: How does Eq. (3) (the optimal policy) follow from the KL-constrained RL objective?
questions.question_body: Equation (3) states $\pi_r(y\mid x)=\frac{1}{Z(x)}\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)\exp\left(\frac{1}{\beta}r(x,y)\right)$. I know this looks like a softmax over actions with a prior, but I'm missing the derivation step from the objective in Eq. (2): $\max_{\pi_\theta} \mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_\theta}[r] - \beta D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_\theta||\pi_{\text{ref}})$. Could someone show the calculus of variations / Lagrangian that gives Eq. (3) or point to the key step?

questions.title: Why does the partition function $Z(x)$ cancel in the Bradley-Terry model when reparameterizing rewards in terms of $\pi$?
questions.question_body: The paper claims that substituting $r(x,y)=\beta\log\frac{\pi(y\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)} + \beta\log Z(x)$ into the BT preference probability causes the $\log Z(x)$ term to cancel because BT depends on reward differences. I roughly see that differences remove additive functions of $x$, but I'd like a concrete algebraic demonstration for two completions $y_1,y_2$ showing that all $Z(x)$ terms drop out and the preference probability depends only on $\pi$ and $\pi_{\text{ref}}$.

questions.title: What is the intuition behind the DPO per-example weight $\sigma(\hat r_\theta(x,y_l)-\hat r_\theta(x,y_w))$ in the gradient?
questions.question_body: In the gradient of the DPO loss the update is multiplied by $\sigma(\hat r_\theta(x,y_l)-\hat r_\theta(x,y_w))$. The authors say it gives higher weight when the implicit reward orders examples incorrectly. But I'm not sure I understand the behavior at extremes: if the model already strongly prefers $y_w$ (so $\hat r(y_w)\gg\hat r(y_l)$), then the weight is near zero and the update is tiny — is that desirable? Conversely, if model strongly prefers the wrong $y_l$, the weight is near 1 and we push hard. How does this weighting balance learning speed and stability compared to unweighted unlikelihood?

questions.title: What exactly is the 'implicit reward' $\hat r_\theta(x,y)$ and why is it equal to $\beta\log\frac{\pi_\theta(y|x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y|x)}$?
questions.question_body: The paper says the language model itself defines an implicit reward via $\hat r_\theta(x,y)=\beta\log\frac{\pi_\theta(y|x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y|x)}$. I understand this comes from rearranging the optimal policy formula, but conceptually: why should the ratio of two policies correspond to reward? Does this imply that every change in probability mass is interpretable as reward? Is there an intuitive explanation linking higher likelihood ratios to higher reward?

questions.title: How should one choose the hyperparameter $\beta$ in practice and what does it control?
questions.question_body: Throughout the paper $\beta$ appears controlling the KL penalty and shows up in the DPO objective and in $\hat r$. But it's unclear how to set it: is $\beta$ analogous to an inverse temperature, to a KL constraint magnitude, or to an Lagrange multiplier? Are there heuristics (e.g. target sequence KL ranges) for choosing $\beta$? What happens if $\beta$ is extremely small or large?

questions.title: Why is DPO equivalent to fitting an explicit reward model up to the equivalence class $r'(x,y)=r(x,y)+f(x)$?
questions.question_body: The paper defines an equivalence relation for rewards that differ by a function of $x$ and claims that DPO's parametrization recovers a representative of each equivalence class. Could someone clarify why adding a function of $x$ doesn't change preferences or optimal policies under the KL objective? I want a short proof/argument that (i) BT preferences depend only on reward differences and (ii) the constrained optimal policy is invariant to $r(x,y)\mapsto r(x,y)+f(x)$.

questions.title: How is the sequence-level KL computed in experiments and why is it the sum of per-token KLs?
questions.question_body: The paper evaluates sequence-level KL defined as 'the sum of the per-timestep KL-divergences'. For autoregressive LMs, is this exactly $\mathrm{KL}(\pi||\pi_{\text{ref}})=\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi}[\sum_t \mathrm{KL}(\pi(\cdot|x,y_{<t})||\pi_{\text{ref}}(\cdot|x,y_{<t}))]$? How do they estimate it in practice (Monte Carlo over samples)? Also, does this measure capture the true KL between sequence distributions or is it only an upper/lower bound?

questions.title: When preference data were generated by a different SFT (distribution shift), how sensitive is DPO to mis-specified $\pi_{\text{ref}}$?
questions.question_body: The paper notes that preference datasets are often sampled using a particular SFT and recommends initializing $\pi_{\text{ref}}=\pi^{\text{SFT}}$ when available. But in many public datasets the SFT that produced data is unknown or different from the model we have. What are practical consequences if $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ used in DPO doesn't match the true data-generating SFT? Is there theory or empirical guidance about robustness to that mismatch?

questions.title: Why does the naive probability-ratio objective cause model degeneration and how does DPO avoid it?
questions.question_body: The authors mention a naive objective that maximizes $\log \frac{\pi(y_w)}{\pi(y_l)}$ without the sigmoid weighting degenerates the LM. What exactly is the degeneration observed (mode collapse? repeating tokens?), and can someone explain intuitively why adding the logistic weight $\sigma(\hat r_\theta(y_l)-\hat r_\theta(y_w))$ prevents this collapse?

questions.title: How does DPO handle preference datasets with more than pairwise comparisons (e.g. ranked lists)?
questions.question_body: The paper briefly says Plackett-Luce models generalize the Bradley-Terry model for ranked answers and that DPO extends there. Concretely, if we have triples or full rankings of $k>2$ candidates per prompt, how is the DPO loss modified? Do we still get a closed-form mapping that cancels partition functions, and what is the resulting classification loss?

questions.title: How do you compute $\log \pi_\theta(y\mid x)$ for long sequences numerically stably in the DPO objective?
questions.question_body: The DPO loss requires computing $\log\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)}$, which for an autoregressive model is a sum of token log-probabilities. For long $y$ the log-prob can be very negative; are there numerical stability concerns or variance issues when optimizing with such long sequence log-prob ratios? Any implementation tricks (per-token clipping, normalization) recommended?

questions.title: How does DPO relate to inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) or energy-based models?
questions.question_body: DPO parameterizes rewards via policy logits and learns from preferences. This reminds me of IRL or energy-based models where you recover a scalar score from behavior. Is DPO theoretically equivalent to a specific IRL formulation? Could the implicit reward $\hat r_\theta$ be interpreted as an energy model, and are there stability/identifiability differences compared to standard IRL?

questions.title: Why does Theorem 1 require 'mild assumptions' and what are they concretely?
questions.question_body: Theorem 1 claims that any reward class compatible with the Plackett-Luce model can be represented as $r(x,y)=\beta\log\frac{\pi(y|x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y|x)}$ for some $\pi$. The sketch proof constructs a projection operator $f$ involving the partition function. Which assumptions about the support of $\pi_{\text{ref}}$, positivity of probabilities, or finiteness of action space are needed for the theorem to hold? Are there pathological cases where the representation fails?

questions.title: Can DPO be applied online (active data collection) or only to offline preference datasets?
questions.question_body: The paper treats a static offline dataset $\mathcal{D}$. If we wanted to run an online loop where we sample completions from the current model, query humans for preferences, and update (like RLHF online), can DPO be used directly each iteration? Are there stability considerations since $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ would change over time?

questions.title: How does DPO compare computationally to PPO and Best-of-$N$ in terms of GPU-hours and memory?
questions.question_body: The paper claims DPO is computationally lightweight and doesn't require sampling in the training loop. Could the authors (or someone) provide ballpark numbers: for training a 6B model on the Anthropic HH dataset, how much less compute did DPO require compared to PPO and Best-of-128? Are there memory overheads from computing both $\pi_\theta$ and $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ log-probs?

questions.title: Why do the authors use GPT-4 as a surrogate human evaluator and how convincing is the human validation study?
questions.question_body: The experiments use GPT-4 to compute win rates and say they validated GPT-4 with a small human study. Given potential evaluator biases (e.g. GPT-4 preferring longer summaries), how reliable are these GPT-4-based comparisons? What was the sample size and inter-annotator agreement of the human validation that supports using GPT-4 as a proxy?

questions.title: How are token-level gradients computed when optimizing the DPO loss that depends on whole-sequence probabilities?
questions.question_body: DPO's loss depends on $\log\pi(y\mid x)$ which is a sum over token log-probs. In implementation, do you compute standard teacher-forced cross-entropy gradients over each token (so per-token teacher forcing) using the sequence as target? Is there any difference compared to supervised fine-tuning backprop for Preferred-FT?

questions.title: Does DPO require that the action space (set of completions) is finite or enumerable?
questions.question_body: Theorem 1 and many derivations sum over $y$ via $\sum_y \pi_{\text{ref}}(y)\exp(\dots)$. For language with an infinite number of possible sequences, how are these sums and the partition function interpreted? Are the results relying on a finite truncation (e.g. beam/sample set), or is it formal via sums over all sequences but practically approximated?

questions.title: What's the relationship between sampling temperature at inference and the DPO training $\beta$?
questions.question_body: The experiments report evaluating models at various sampling temperatures. Is there a principled relationship between the DPO training parameter $\beta$ and the sampling temperature (which rescales logits at inference)? For instance, if I trained with a small $\beta$, should I pick a lower/higher sampling temperature? Any guidance on how they interacted in experiments?

questions.title: How does DPO behave if the true human preference model is not Bradley-Terry (BT)?
questions.question_body: The derivation uses BT (a logistic function of reward differences). Human annotators might use other non-BT decision processes or be inconsistent. If the data-generating preference model deviates from BT, does DPO still learn a reasonable policy? Are there robustness guarantees or ways to generalize DPO to other preference noise models?

questions.title: In Eq. (11) the authors enforce $\sum_y \pi_{\text{ref}}(y)\exp(\frac{1}{\beta}r(x,y))=1$. Why is that justified and what does it mean?
questions.question_body: Equation (11) states the DPO projection produces reward functions satisfying $\sum_y \pi_{\text{ref}}(y)\exp(\frac{1}{\beta}r(x,y))=1$. That looks like a normalization choice. But can we always enforce that? Does this choice restrict the expressive power of rewards? How do I intuitively interpret picking the member of the reward equivalence class that makes this sum equal to 1?

questions.title: How exactly is the 'Best of $N$' baseline implemented and why is it computationally impractical?
questions.question_body: The paper compares to 'Best of $N$' which samples $N$ completions and returns the top-scoring by a learned reward. Is the cost only at inference since you must generate $N$ samples per prompt? Are there additional training costs? How does Best-of-$N$ performance scale with $N$ empirically and why did they choose 128 for dialogue?

questions.title: Can DPO be used to optimize for safety-related attributes (e.g. toxicity) and how does it avoid reward hacking?
questions.question_body: The paper reports sentiment/summarization/dialogue tasks. If we collect preferences for 'non-toxic' responses, can DPO be used analogously? Given the implicit reward is tied to $\pi_\theta/\pi_{\text{ref}}$, could DPO produce adversarial sequences that exploit the implicit reward or the evaluator (reward hacking)? Any empirical evidence or recommendations about safeguards?

questions.title: Where are the proofs for Lemma 1, Lemma 2, and Theorem 1 located and what are their main proof ideas?
questions.question_body: The paper references proofs deferred to appendices but I don't see them here. Could someone summarize the proof strategies for Lemma 1 (two rewards in same equivalence class induce same preferences), Lemma 2 (same optimal policy), and Theorem 1 (representation of reward classes by DPO parametrization)? What are the nontrivial steps to watch out for?

questions.title: Why does the DPO gradient have a multiplicative factor of $-\beta$ and could we absorb $\beta$ into learning rate?
questions.question_body: The gradient of the DPO loss includes a $-\beta$ factor out front. Is that purely because of the parameterization of $\hat r_\theta$? In practice could we just drop this scalar and tune the optimizer learning rate accordingly, or does keeping $\beta$ explicitly in the gradient change the training dynamics qualitatively?
